source.title: Continuous Autoregressive Language Models
source.authors: Chen-Ze Shao; Darren Li; Fan-Dong Meng; Jie Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports model-size comparisons using BrierLM, but does not test any listed version of the scaling-law claim. Its references to scaling laws are not tests or reliance on the claimed laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports BrierLM scores and compute for several model sizes, and describes training curves, but does not fit or test held-out cross-entropy power laws, extrapolate from smaller runs, or search for compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. BrierLM scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version because they are not the cross-entropy measure named in the versions. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces CALM, a continuous next-vector language model, and cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation and future work. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing, and does not search for compute-optimal allocations. Its scale comparison spans about 3x in parameters (281M–849M Transformers), is measured in BrierLM rather than held-out cross-entropy, and has no functional fit, so it does not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CALM gives a better performance-compute trade-off than discrete Transformer baselines. They name a unified scaling law including semantic bandwidth K as future work.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction or direct test of the original scaling-law method is performed; the model-scale comparison uses BrierLM and compute rather than fitted held-out cross-entropy laws.

fits_no_version.finding: BrierLM rises with model size for both Transformer (6.05→7.07→8.98) and CALM K=4 (5.72→6.58→8.53). The authors say CALM 'benefits from scaling just as effectively' as Transformers. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A likelihood-free sample-based LM metric (BrierLM) improves monotonically with model size and training compute, for both discrete-token and continuous-vector autoregressive LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 shows the chunk size K shifting CALM-L's performance-compute position relative to the Transformer size curve. K=4 beats the baseline frontier and K=8 drops in performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokens per generative step (semantic bandwidth) acts as an additional scaling axis on the performance-compute frontier.

record.problems: The reported model-scale comparison uses BrierLM rather than held-out cross-entropy and does not fit scaling exponents or test extrapolation. Numerical uncertainty estimates are not reported for Table 1.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 gives qualitative training-curve descriptions and Figure 4 compares chunk sizes and compute, but neither reports a result testing a listed claim version; no additional rows were extracted.

untested.parts: Power-law fit of held-out cross-entropy against parameters, tokens or compute over orders of magnitude. Only three Transformer sizes spanning about 3x are reported, in BrierLM, with no fit.
Extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task predictability from scale or loss.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 3 plots BrierLM against cross-entropy for Transformer S/M/L checkpoints (Pearson -0.966). That validates the metric, not a scaling law, so no row is needed. The training curves in Figure 5 are qualitative. cites_only/T6 is appropriate; 'discusses' would also be defensible, given the future-work paragraph on scaling laws with K as a third variable.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small runs to substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, including departures from a single power law.
